newsitem.title: BULGARIA: U.S ADVISOR URGES BULGARIA NOT TO FIX LEV FOR LONG.
newsitem.headline: U.S ADVISOR URGES BULGARIA NOT TO FIX LEV FOR LONG.

text.p: A U.S. economist warned Bulgaria on Monday against a long-term implementation of a fixed exchange rate regime proposed by the International Monetary Fund to help stabilise the Balkan country's crumbling economy.

"What I believe is that the currency board is a good idea, but it is important to understand that it is a solution that needs to move to a more flexible system in the longer term," economist Jeffrey Sachs told a news conference.
Speaking after a four-day visit to Bulgaria as economic advisor to President Petar Stoyanov, Sachs, director of the Harvard Institute of Development said:

"The basic idea of the currency board is to stabilise the curency and get international backing for it, and have a tight credit policy. All these are sound principles for stabilising the currency and ending hyper-inflation."

Sachs's visit coincided with an IMF mission in Sofia, which is negotiating with the interim cabinet a new funding agreement aimed to help the country stabilise its sinking national currency and ailing banks.

The currency board would require levs in circulation to be matched by central bank reserves, severely curbing the financial powers of the government and the central bank, thus preventing the printing of money.
The programme, which the cabinet hopes to complete by the end of this week, will also contain amendments to bank laws designed jointly with the IMF to enable the introduction of the currency board.
"What I am against is the perception that you can change the law and fix the exchange rate forever, lock it up and throw away the key and think that the country can run on autopilot," said Sachs.

The IMF mission presented agreement proposals to the cabinet last week, urging the caretaker government to finalise its 1997 draft budget, and work out details of the financial stabilisation policy, social safety nets and structural reform.
"We have full agreement on the general principles, now we have to work out the details," said an IMF official who declined to be named.

Sachs, who has helped Russian and Polish governments get on the road to economic reform, is holding a meeting of Bulgarian and international economic experts at Harvard University this week to contiue working on detailed issues of economic reform.

Bulgaria, which relies solely on external support to repay $1 billion debts due this year alone, stands to win more funding from other lenders like the European Union and the World Bank, once an IMF deal is in place. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
